title: Why AI Is More Assistant Than Replacement
title_hi: Why AI Is More Assistant Than Replacement
summary: Every few months, a new headline claims that artificial intelligence is about to replace millions of jobs. It sounds dra
content:
Every few months, a new headline claims that artificial intelligence is about to replace millions of jobs. It sounds dramatic, and it gets clicks. But if you spend time using AI in real work, the picture looks very different.

AI is changing how we work. It is not replacing work itself.

For most people, AI behaves less like a replacement and more like a very fast assistant. It helps with repetitive tasks, drafting, organizing, summarizing, and searching for information. The human still decides what matters, what is correct, and what should be done next.

That distinction is more important than it seems.


  
  
  The difference between tasks and jobs


A job is not a single task.

A customer support agent does not only answer questions. They calm frustrated customers, understand context, make judgment calls, and know when to escalate a problem.

A marketer does not only write captions. They understand the audience, the brand, timing, and business goals.

A teacher does not only explain information. They motivate, adapt, encourage, and notice when a student is struggling.

AI can assist with some tasks inside these jobs. It rarely replaces the entire job.

This is why many people who use AI daily are not becoming unemployed. They are becoming faster.


  
  
  What AI is genuinely good at


Here are the areas where AI already provides obvious value:


Summarizing meetings and documents
Drafting emails and reports
Organizing notes and information
Generating first versions of content
Translating and rewriting text
Searching across large amounts of data
Automating repetitive digital workflows
These are valuable capabilities, but notice the pattern: most of them remove friction.


AI is often taking away the tedious part of work, not the meaningful part.


  
  
  The calculator lesson


When calculators became common, people feared that mathematics would become unnecessary.

The opposite happened.

Calculators removed the need to do long arithmetic by hand, which allowed people to focus on algebra, statistics, engineering, finance, and science. The tool did not eliminate mathematical thinking; it increased the value of higher-level thinking.

AI is creating a similar shift.

If an AI drafts a rough report in 30 seconds, the valuable skill is no longer typing the first draft. The valuable skill becomes knowing what the report should say, what evidence matters, and whether the conclusion is sound.


  
  
  Where humans still dominate


Current AI systems are impressive, but they still struggle with several things that are central to many professions.

Judgment
Choosing between two reasonable options based on incomplete information.

Responsibility
Humans are accountable for decisions. AI is not.

Creativity with constraints
Generating ideas that fit a specific culture, audience, or business situation.

Trust
People trust people, especially in healthcare, education, law, leadership, and relationships.

Adaptability
Handling unexpected situations that were not part of the original prompt or workflow.

These are not small details. They are often the core of professional value.

A practical example
Imagine a small business owner.

Without AI:


Takes notes during a client call
Writes a follow-up email
Updates the CRM
Creates a task list
Prepares a short summary for the team


With AI:


AI transcribes the call
AI drafts the follow-up
AI suggests CRM updates
AI extracts action items
AI generates a summary
What disappeared?


Mostly administrative work.

What remained?

Building the relationship, negotiating, deciding priorities, and closing the deal.

The business owner was not replaced. The busywork was reduced.


  
  
  Why the replacement narrative is so popular


Predictions about total replacement are easier to tell than nuanced reality.

“AI will change workflows” is accurate but boring.

“AI will replace everyone” is exciting.

Historically, technology has usually done three things:


Eliminated some tasks
Changed many jobs
Created new kinds of work


The internet reduced some jobs, transformed many others, and created roles that barely existed before: social media managers, app developers, SEO specialists, content creators, cloud architects, and many more.

AI is likely to follow the same pattern.


  
  
  The real risk is not AI


A useful way to think about it is this:

The biggest risk is often not being replaced by AI; it is being outperformed by someone who knows how to use AI well.

Two designers with equal talent may produce different amounts of work if one can use AI for ideation and iteration.

Two analysts may differ if one can automate data cleanup and summarization.

Two entrepreneurs may differ if one can use AI to handle repetitive operations.

The competitive advantage comes from human + AI, not AI alone.


  
  
  How to work with AI instead of fearing it


If you want to stay valuable, focus on the skills that become more important as AI improves.

1. Learn to ask better questions: Clear prompts lead to better outputs.

2. Verify everything important: AI can be confidently wrong.

3. Develop domain expertise: Knowledge of your field becomes more valuable, not less.

4. Improve communication: Explaining decisions and persuading people remains a human strength.

5. Automate the repetitive parts: Protect your energy for work that requires judgment and creativity.

A better mental model

Think of AI as a junior assistant who is incredibly fast, never gets tired, and can process huge amounts of information.

That assistant can:


Prepare drafts
Collect information
Organize data
Suggest ideas
Handle repetitive steps


But you still need someone to:


Set the goal
Judge quality
Make decisions
Take responsibility
Understand people


That someone is human.


  
  
  The bottom line


AI will absolutely change the workplace. Some roles will shrink, some will evolve, and new ones will appear. Pretending nothing is changing would be a mistake.

But treating AI as a complete replacement for human work is also a mistake. For most professionals today, AI is best understood as a multiplier.

It multiplies speed, it multiplies access to information, it multiplies output. It does not automatically multiply judgment, responsibility, empathy, or wisdom. And those qualities are still what turn work into value.

The future of work is unlikely to be humans versus AI. It is much more likely to be humans with AI versus humans without it.

title: How I Cut My API Costs by 60% With a 50-Line Python Cache
title_hi: How I Cut My API Costs by 60% With a 50-Line Python Cache
summary:
How I Cut My API Costs by 60% With a 50-Line Python Cache


Last month I got a bill from an AI API provider tha
content:
How I Cut My API Costs by 60% With a 50-Line Python Cache


Last month I got a bill from an AI API provider that made me choke on my coffee. $340. For a side project that maybe 50 people use.

The culprit? I was calling the same endpoints with the same parameters over and over. Every user refresh hit the API. Every page reload. Every test run.

I checked the logs and found something embarrassing: 73% of my API calls were identical duplicates — same endpoint, same payload, same response.

That's when I built this. It took 30 minutes and I haven't touched it since. Here's the code, why it works, and the one edge case that almost broke everything.


  
  
  The Problem, Quantified


Before I show you the code, here's what my API usage looked like:




Metric
Before
After




Daily API calls
8,400
2,300


Duplicate call rate
73%
12%


Monthly bill
$340
$135


Avg response time
1.2s
80ms




The 12% that still slip through are dynamic queries — things like "what's the weather right now" where caching makes no sense. Everything else gets served from disk.


  
  
  The Code


Here's the full thing. 50 lines of Python, no dependencies outside the standard library:



import hashlib
import json
import os
import time
from functools import wraps

CACHE_DIR = "./api_cache"
DEFAULT_TTL = 3600  # 1 hour


def _make_key(method: str, url: str, params: dict, body: dict) -> str:
    """Create a deterministic cache key from request components."""
    payload = json.dumps({
        "m": method,
        "u": url,
        "p": sorted(params.items()) if params else [],
        "b": sorted(body.items()) if body else [],
    }, sort_keys=True)
    return hashlib.sha256(payload.encode()).hexdigest()


def _path(key: str) -> str:
    return os.path.join(CACHE_DIR, key[:2], key)


def api_cache(ttl: int = DEFAULT_TTL):
    """Cache API responses to disk with configurable TTL."""

    def decorator(func):
        @wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            # Extract identifiable request components
            # Adjust these based on how YOUR API client works
            req = kwargs.get("request_data", {})
            key = _make_key(
                method=req.get("method", "GET"),
                url=req.get("url", func.__name__),
                params=req.get("params", {}),
                body=req.get("body", {}),
            )

            cache_path = _path(key)

            # Cache hit — check freshness
            if os.path.exists(cache_path):
                age = time.time() - os.path.getmtime(cache_path)
                if age < ttl:
                    with open(cache_path, "r") as f:
                        return json.load(f)

            # Cache miss — call the real API
            result = func(*args, **kwargs)

            # Don't cache errors. This is the part I got wrong the first time.
            if result and not isinstance(result, Exception):
                os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(cache_path), exist_ok=True)
                with open(cache_path, "w") as f:
                    json.dump(result, f)

            return result

        return wrapper
    return decorator







  
  
  How to Use It


Wrap your API call function and pass in request metadata:



import requests

@api_cache(ttl=1800)  # 30 minutes
def call_openai(prompt: str, request_data: dict = None):
    resp = requests.post(
        "https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENAI_KEY']}"},
        json={
            "model": "gpt-4o-mini",
            "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        },
    )
    return resp.json()


# Call it — first time hits the API, subsequent calls in the
# next 30 minutes return from cache
result = call_openai(
    "summarize this text: ...",
    request_data={
        "method": "POST",
        "url": "openai/chat/completions",
        "params": {},
        "body": {"prompt": "summarize this text: ..."},
    },
)






For more complex APIs, include the relevant distinguishing fields in request_data.body. The hash function handles the rest.


  
  
  The Edge Case I Got Wrong


On day one, I cached everything. Including errors.

My AI provider went down for 8 minutes. During that window, my cache stored 429 responses — HTTP errors — and served them to every user for the full TTL. Users saw "rate limit exceeded" for things that normally worked fine.

That's why there's this check in the code:



if result and not isinstance(result, Exception):
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(cache_path), exist_ok=True)
    ...






Two rules I now follow:


Never cache 4xx or 5xx responses.

Never cache empty responses. They hide real outages.


If you're wrapping requests, here's a quick filter you can add:



def _is_cacheable(response) -> bool:
    if response is None:
        return False
    if isinstance(response, dict) and "error" in response:
        return False
    # If using requests.Response object
    if hasattr(response, "status_code") and response.status_code >= 400:
        return False
    return True







  
  
  When NOT to Use This


This works well for:


AI text generation with deterministic prompts (same prompt = same response)
REST API read endpoints (GET /users/42)
Configuration fetches
Anything where staleness is acceptable for a few minutes


It does not work for:


Real-time data (stock prices, live sports scores)
Write operations (POST that creates resources)
User-specific data unless you include user ID in the cache key
Endpoints with rapidly changing state


I learned that last one the hard way when I cached a "current server status" endpoint and spent an afternoon debugging why my dashboard showed "healthy" for a server that had been down for two hours.


  
  
  Going Further: Memory + Disk


The version above uses disk only. That's fine for hundreds of requests per minute. If you need more speed, add an in-memory LRU layer first:



from collections import OrderedDict

_mem_cache: OrderedDict[str, tuple[float, dict]] = OrderedDict()
MAX_MEM_ITEMS = 500

def _cache_get(key: str, ttl: int) -> dict | None:
    # Check memory first
    if key in _mem_cache:
        ts, val = _mem_cache[key]
        if time.time() - ts < ttl:
            _mem_cache.move_to_end(key)
            return val
        del _mem_cache[key]

    # Fall back to disk
    cache_path = _path(key)
    if os.path.exists(cache_path):
        age = time.time() - os.path.getmtime(cache_path)
        if age < ttl:
            with open(cache_path) as f:
                val = json.load(f)
            _mem_cache[key] = (time.time(), val)
            if len(_mem_cache) > MAX_MEM_ITEMS:
                _mem_cache.popitem(last=False)
            return val

    return None






This adds about 15 lines and makes cache hits virtually instant. For my use case the disk-only version was enough, but if you're serving web traffic, the memory layer is worth it.


  
  
  What I'd Do Differently


If I were building this again from scratch:



Use SQLite instead of files. Better concurrent access, built-in TTL with a timestamp column, and one file instead of thousands.

Add cache statistics. Hit rate, miss rate, total bytes saved. I ended up adding this later anyway to justify the build to myself.

Make TTL configurable per endpoint. Some endpoints are fine at 1 hour, others need 5 minutes.


But honestly? The 50-line version has been running untouched for a month and saved me $205. Sometimes the simple thing is good enough.




Have you built something similar? What's your approach to API cost control? I'd love to hear about it in the comments.

  Build a deterministic prompt function





function promptFor(system, item) {
  return [
    `Create one ${item.object}.`,
    `Canvas ${system.canvas}; background ${system.background}.`,
    `Use ${system.stroke}; accent ${item.accent}.`,
    `${system.lighting}.`,
    `Do not include ${system.forbidden.join(', ')}.`
  ].join(' ')
}






Keep order stable so prompt diffs stay reviewable. Do not inject random style adjectives between rows.


  
  
  Pilot before the batch


Generate two contrasting items first. The current GPT Image 2 default family estimate observed today was 4 credits, but size/model changes can alter it; confirm the live estimate and public-visibility setting before Generate. If the pilot fails, edit the contract rather than patching each item separately.


  
  
  Validator





const required = ['canvas', 'background', 'stroke', 'lighting'];
function validateRow(row) {
  const missing = required.filter(k => !row.system?.[k]);
  if (missing.length) throw new Error(`Missing: ${missing.join(', ')}`);
  if (!/^#[0-9A-F]{6}$/i.test(row.item.accent)) throw new Error('Bad accent');
}






Visual QA still needs humans. Check canvas, background, stroke weight, object count, forbidden text, and semantic accuracy. Record pass/fail by item ID.


  
  
  Troubleshooting


Style drifts: move the shared style block to the beginning and remove synonyms.
Objects multiply: say “one centered object” and reject extra props.
Colors mutate: provide exact hex values plus color names.
One item needs a special exception: add an explicit exceptions field; do not silently change the global contract.


  
  
  Limits


This is not a transactional batch API: generation may remain variable, and exact pixel identity is not guaranteed. The current model, credit estimate, and availability can change. Public is the current default, so switch it for confidential assets. Generated icons also require license, trademark, and accessibility review.

Once the matrix passes validation, run the small pilot in the exact bulk workspace.
